title: Ganesh Chaturthi: Ganpati Bappa Morya
hookLine: an old devotee who can't walk to the temple anymore, and why the crowds shout his name with Ganesha's
carry: bhakti: god walks toward you too
last: YOGAMAYA: GOD HIDES IN PLAIN SIGHT.

cards: The last day of Ganesh Chaturthi in Pune or Mumbai. The clay Ganesha is lifted onto a cart, the drums start, and the whole street walks him to the water, shouting one line over and over: Ganpati Bappa Morya!
Bappa is Marathi for father. So the crowd is calling God Dad. But who is Morya?
He isn't a god. He was a man, a devotee, and huge crowds shout his name with Ganesha's every year. Here's how that happened.

teach.b: Morya Gosavi lived centuries ago near Pune, and he loved Ganesha. As the Chinchwad tradition tells it, every month he walked from his home at Chinchwad to Ganesha's temple at Morgaon, a long way on foot, year after year.
Then he grew old, and the walk became too much. He was heartbroken. What is a devotee who can't reach the temple anymore?

teach.h: DON'T WORRY. I'LL COME TO YOU.
teach.b: The tradition says Ganesha came to him in a dream: don't worry. I'll come to you.
Soon after, bathing in the river at Morgaon, Morya found a small stone image of Ganesha in the water, carried it home to Chinchwad, and built a temple for it there.

The devotee couldn't make the journey, so God made it instead. People say Morya's love was so complete that his name and Ganesha's became one cry: Ganpati Bappa Morya. That's the teaching inside the chant.
In bhakti, the path of loving devotion, the love runs both ways. The devotee walks toward God, and God walks toward the devotee. Close enough to call Bappa, Dad.
Close enough that a devotee's name gets shouted with his. And it's why Ganesh Chaturthi works the way it does.

teach.h: GANESHA COMES HOME AS A GUEST.
teach.b: Families don't only go to the temple; they bring Ganesha home as a guest, for a day and a half, or five days, or ten. Then at the water they shout the rest of the line, in Marathi: pudhchya varshi lavkar ya.
Come back soon next year. You don't say that to a distant god. You say it to someone who has come to your house, and who you know will come again.

teach.h: BHAKTI: GOD WALKS TOWARD YOU TOO.
teach.b: Bhakti: God walks toward you too.

how: During Ganesh Chaturthi many Hindu families bring a clay Ganesha home as a guest for a day and a half up to ten days, and at the immersion, especially in Maharashtra, crowds shout 'Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya': come back soon next year.

o: Ganesha's festival on the fourth day

games.q: who's who in the chant — tap the pairs.
p: the devotee whose name joins Ganesha's

s: the Morya in the chant was the name of Ganesha's mouse
Morya Gosavi was a man, a devotee; people say his love joined his name to Ganesha's cry.
when Morya couldn't walk to the temple anymore, Ganesha came to him
as the Chinchwad tradition tells it, Morya found Ganesha's image in the river and carried him home.
at the immersion, families say goodbye to Ganesha forever
they shout 'come back soon next year': he's a guest who'll return.

games.q: you're Morya, old now, and you can't walk to Morgaon anymore. in the story, what happens?
o: you stop worshipping. the temple's too far.
you send a younger man to pray for you.
games.why: in a dream Ganesha says: I'll come to you. bhakti runs both ways: the devotee walks toward God, and God walks toward the devotee.

practice: If you pray, picture Ganesha arriving at your door the way families welcome him, with drums and flowers, and say softly, three times: Ganpati Bappa Morya. Then, before you open your eyes, say the second half: come back soon.
If you don't pray, think of someone who came to you when you couldn't get to them, and say their name, with thanks. Breathe, and let them in.

wordCard.voice: Ganesh Chaturthi. Ganesha's festival on the fourth day, when he comes home as a guest, and the crowds call him Bappa.

orig.note: Marathi: father, dad; the crowd's name for Ganesha in Ganpati Bappa Morya.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti: god walks toward you too. When Morya couldn't come, Ganesha came to him. Ninety-three down.
